question: In obstructive jaundice, bleeding tendency is due to deficiency of the following clotting factors, except:
summary_line: Obstructive jaundice -> down Vitamin K -> down II, VII, IX, X

scenes.heading: Question
scenes.narration: Here's the question. In obstructive jaundice, a bleeding tendency develops due to deficiency of several clotting factors -- except one. Your options are factor two, factor seven, factor eight, factor nine, and factor ten. Take a moment, then let's work through the mechanism together.
scenes.caption: In obstructive jaundice, bleeding tendency is due to deficiency of the following clotting factors, except:

scenes.heading: The Mechanism -- Why Bleeding Happens at All
scenes.narration: Let's start with why obstructive jaundice causes bleeding in the first place. Obstructive jaundice means bile can't flow from the liver into the small intestine -- the path is blocked, usually by a gallstone in the common bile duct, a tumor, or a stricture. Bile is essential for digesting and absorbing fat, and along with fat, it carries the fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, and K. No bile reaching the gut means poor absorption of vitamin K. And vitamin K is not optional here -- it's a required cofactor the liver uses to activate four specific clotting factors: two, seven, nine, and ten. Without vitamin K, the liver still makes these factors, but they come out non-functional. The result is a bleeding tendency, even though the liver itself is working fine.
scenes.caption: Bile blocked -> fat & Vitamin K malabsorption -> inactive clotting factors

scenes.heading: The Vitamin K-Dependent Factors
scenes.narration: This is the key fact the whole question is built on. Only four clotting factors depend on vitamin K to become active: factor two, which is prothrombin, factor seven, factor nine, and factor ten. A simple way to remember them is the number nineteen seventy-two -- factors one thousand nine, seven, two -- read as nine, seven, two... it's easier to just remember the set: two, seven, nine, ten. Every one of these drops when vitamin K can't be absorbed. Factor eight is not on this list, and that difference is exactly what this question is testing.
scenes.caption: Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X

scenes.heading: Why A, B, D, and E Are Wrong
scenes.narration: Let's go through the wrong options one at a time, and I mean truly wrong for this question -- not bad facts, just the wrong answer to what's being asked. Factor two, prothrombin: this is vitamin K-dependent, so it IS reduced in obstructive jaundice. Since the question asks for the one that is the exception, factor two does not qualify -- it behaves exactly like the others. Factor seven: same story. It's vitamin K-dependent, it drops early because it has the shortest half-life of the group, and it's part of the expected pattern here -- not the exception. Factor nine: vitamin K-dependent as well, so it's reduced right along with the rest -- again, not the exception. Factor ten: also vitamin K-dependent, also reduced. So four of your five options -- two, seven, nine, and ten -- all share the same mechanism: they need vitamin K to work, vitamin K isn't getting absorbed, so all four are low. None of them can be the exception, because none of them is behaving differently from the rest.
scenes.caption: II, VII, IX, X are ALL vitamin K-dependent -> all reduced -> none is the exception

scenes.heading: Why Factor VIII Is the Exception
scenes.narration: Now factor eight -- the actual answer. Factor eight is fundamentally different from the other four, and here's why. It is not vitamin K-dependent at all. It doesn't need that activation step. And it isn't made primarily by liver hepatocytes the way the vitamin K-dependent factors are -- it's produced mainly by vascular endothelial cells, the cells lining your blood vessels, all over the body, not just in the liver. So when bile flow is blocked and vitamin K absorption drops, factor eight is simply unaffected by that pathway. In fact, in obstructive jaundice, factor eight is often normal, or even elevated, because it behaves somewhat like an acute-phase protein during inflammation or cholestasis. That is precisely why it's the exception: every other option shares the vitamin K mechanism, and factor eight sits completely outside it.
scenes.caption: Factor VIII: NOT vitamin K-dependent, made by endothelium -> stays normal or rises

scenes.heading: Clinical Pearl -- Telling Vitamin K Deficiency from True Liver Failure
scenes.narration: Here's a genuinely useful clinical pearl that extends this concept. If a patient has a bleeding tendency and you want to know whether it's from vitamin K deficiency or cholestasis, versus true liver failure, check factor five. Factor five, like factor eight, is not vitamin K-dependent -- so it stays normal in simple vitamin K deficiency. But unlike factor eight, factor five IS made exclusively by liver hepatocytes. So in real liver failure, where the liver has lost its synthetic function altogether, factor five drops, while in obstructive jaundice with intact liver cells, factor five stays normal. That single factor is often the clue that separates a plumbing problem, a blocked bile duct, from an actual liver factory problem.
scenes.caption: Factor V normal = vitamin K problem. Factor V low = true liver failure.

scenes.heading: Take-Home
scenes.narration: Let's lock this in. Obstructive jaundice blocks bile, bile is needed to absorb vitamin K, and vitamin K activates factors two, seven, nine, and ten. All four of those drop. Factor eight doesn't depend on vitamin K and isn't purely liver-made, so it stays normal -- making it the exception, and the correct answer to this question. The final answer is C, factor eight.
scenes.caption: Correct answer: C -- Factor VIII (not vitamin K-dependent)
